reason: A opens inside the Naseby fight and then carries a second sustained narrative through the siege of Constantinople, so the analytical material about arsenals, ledgers and Tokugawa control arrives attached to people and events the reader already cares about. B front-loads an inventory and then strings together Selim III, the taille, Dutch bonds, Mughal ranks, Nagashima and the English Civil War as short survey blocks, and holds its one vivid scene (Magdeburg) until the final pages. B also restates its thesis repeatedly - that the debate should follow invoices and rosters, that technology widened reach while rulers chose targets - which flattens the sense of movement, whereas A states that conclusion once, at the end.
